did_you_know.text: Did you know? Abijah became king of Judah in the eighteenth year of Jeroboam’s reign, and he ruled in Jerusalem for three years.
Did you know? According to the numbers given in the chapter, Judah’s army numbered 400,000 men, while Jeroboam’s army numbered 800,000—twice as many.

Did you know? Abijah claimed that the kingship over Israel had been given to David and his descendants through a “covenant of salt”—a term used here to describe a permanent covenant between the Lord and the house of David.

Did you know? Abijah criticized Jeroboam for replacing the priests descended from Aaron and the Levites with priests appointed from among the people. He even described their qualifications: one young bull and seven rams.

Did you know? In his speech, Abijah described worship in Judah’s temple: burnt offerings offered morning and evening, the burning of incense, the bread arranged on the table, and the lighting of the golden lampstand.
Did you know? Jeroboam tried to defeat Judah by sending an ambush around to the rear, so that Judah’s army found itself facing the enemy both in front and behind.
Did you know? When the men of Judah shouted and the priests blew the trumpets, the chapter describes the victory as the result of the Lord defeating Jeroboam and Israel.
Did you know? After the victory, Abijah captured several cities and settlements from Jeroboam, including Bethel, Jeshanah, and Ephron, along with the surrounding settlements.
Did you know? Abijah had fourteen wives, who bore him twenty-two sons and sixteen daughters. After his death, Asa succeeded him, and the land had peace for ten years during Asa’s reign.
